definitions.text: Biochemistry is the study of the chemical processes that occur within living organisms (e.g., photosynthesis, cellular respiration).
Molecular biology is the study of the structure and function of the biomolecules (e.g., carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids).
The molecules produced by organisms are called biomolecules or biological molecules.
All the chemical reactions that occur in an organism are collectively called metabolism.
Anabolism is the type of metabolism in which simpler substances are combined to form complex substances. Energy is used in these reactions.
Catabolism is the type of metabolism in which complex molecules are broken down into simpler ones. Energy is released in these reactions.
They are the organic compounds in which the ratio of H and O is 2:1 (same as in water).
Monosaccharides (simple sugars) are made of single sugar molecule. They are easily soluble in water and have sweet taste.
They are made of two monosaccharides units. They are less soluble in water and are less sweet in taste.
Polysaccharides are large molecules composed of hundreds to thousands of monosaccharides units. They are insoluble in water and are tasteless.
They are defined as the polymers of amino acids.
Amino acids are the organic molecules that join in specific number and sequence to make proteins.
Essential amino acids: These are the 09 amino acids which cannot be synthesized by our body and are supplied by foods.
Non-essential amino acids: These are 11 amino acids that can be synthesised in our bodies.
An amino acid is an organic molecule made of an amino group (NH₂), a carboxyl group (COOH), a hydrogen group (H) and a side group (R) which are attached to a central carbon atom:
Lipids are organic compounds that are insoluble in water but are soluble in organic solvents (e.g., alcohol, ether, benzene).
Glycerol is an alcohol having 3 carbon atoms. Each carbon has a hydroxyl group.
Fatty acids are long hydrocarbon chains with carboxyl group (COOH) at the end.
Saturated fatty acids have internal carbon atoms bonded with maximum number of hydrogen atoms. They do not have double bonds between carbon atoms. Saturated fatty acids are solid at room temperature.
Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more double bonds between carbon atoms. They are liquid at room temperature.
Fats and oils are the most familiar lipids. They contain one glycerol and three fatty acids.
Nucleic acids are the biomolecules that are composed of units called nucleotides.

The segment of DNA in which the sequence of nucleotides determines the synthesis of a protein (polypeptide chain) is called a gene.
RNA is single-stranded. Its strand consists of ribonucleotides. A ribonucleotide contains ribose sugar instead of deoxyribose.
The process of making mRNA copy of DNA is called transcription.
The ribosome reads this sequence and joins specific amino acids to form a protein. This step is known as translation.

fullMarks: For the three carbohydrate groups, state the number of sugar units first, then solubility and taste; include one correct example if the question asks for structures or roles.
For an amino-acid drawing, show a central carbon attached to NH₂, COOH, H and R, and label all four groups clearly.
For lipid structures, distinguish glycerol from fatty acids; show three fatty acids in fats and oils, but two fatty acids and a phosphate group in a phospholipid.

When explaining fatty-acid types, mention the carbon-to-carbon bonds and the state at room temperature: saturated has no double bonds and is solid; unsaturated has one or more double bonds and is liquid.
For DNA, write the two strands and double-helix arrangement, then state A–T and C–G pairing and the correct hydrogen-bond counts.
For a functions question, give each function as a separate point and pair it with a specific example where possible, such as haemoglobin transporting oxygen or antibodies defending against pathogens.
For DNA function, connect the nucleotide sequence to the amino-acid order in a protein and state that DNA passes hereditary information to the next generation.
mistakes: Mistake: Saying polysaccharides are sweet or water-soluble. Fix: They are tasteless and insoluble in water.
Mistake: Confusing the storage polysaccharides of plants and animals. Fix: Starch is stored in plants; glycogen is mainly stored in the liver and muscles of animals.
Mistake: Drawing an amino acid without its R group or central carbon. Fix: Attach NH₂, COOH, H and R to the same central carbon.
Mistake: Saying saturated fatty acids have double bonds. Fix: Saturated fatty acids have no carbon-to-carbon double bonds; unsaturated fatty acids have one or more.
Mistake: Drawing fats and oils with only two fatty acids. Fix: Show one glycerol and three fatty acids; two fatty acids plus phosphate describes a phospholipid.
Mistake: Pairing adenine with cytosine, or giving the wrong bond count. Fix: A pairs with T using two hydrogen bonds; C pairs with G using three.
Mistake: Mixing up transcription and translation. Fix: Transcription copies DNA information into mRNA; translation uses mRNA at a ribosome to make a protein.

shortTheory.question: Short 6.2: How do the three group of carbohydrates differ in taste?
shortTheory.answer: Monosaccharides have sweet taste. Disaccharides are less sweet in taste. Polysaccharides are tasteless.

shortTheory.question: Short 6.3: Name two common monosaccharides and two disaccharides.
shortTheory.answer: Two common monosaccharides are glucose and fructose. Two disaccharides are sucrose and maltose.

shortTheory.question: Short 6.5: Give an example of a storage polysaccharide in plants.
shortTheory.answer: Starch is a storage polysaccharide found in plants.

shortTheory.question: Short 6.6: Define amino acid and draw its structure.
shortTheory.answer: An amino acid is an organic molecule made of an amino group (NH₂), a carboxyl group (COOH), a hydrogen group (H) and a side group (R) which are attached to a central carbon atom. Structure: H₂N—C(H)(R)—COOH.

shortTheory.question: Short 6.8: What are the types of RNA? Write their functions.
shortTheory.answer: Messenger RNA (mRNA) carries the genetic information from DNA to the ribosomes during protein synthesis. Transfer RNA (tRNA) transfers specific amino acids to the ribosomes, ensuring the correct sequence during protein synthesis. Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) constitutes the structural and functional components of ribosomes, the cellular machinery for protein synthesis.

shortTheory.question: Short 6.9: Briefly describe the function of DNA.
shortTheory.answer: DNA contains the hereditary information. This information is in the form of a sequence of nucleotides. This sequence determines the order of amino acids during protein synthesis. During reproduction, DNA is passed from one generation to the next.
